A technical SEO audit checklist for small-business websites

Check crawlability, canonical URLs, metadata, structured data, performance, accessibility, and indexable-page quality before prioritizing SEO fixes.

By TurboApply6 min read
On this page
Confirm crawl and index controls Check page-level search signals Test speed, mobile layout, and accessibility Turn findings into a repair sequence

A technical SEO audit should turn a long list of checks into a short, evidence-based repair plan. Start with whether important pages can be found and understood, then prioritize issues that affect customers or create conflicting search signals.

Confirm crawl and index controls

List every intended public page and compare it with the sitemap, internal links, robots rules, canonical tags, and live HTTP status. Important pages should not depend on a hidden or broken path to be discovered.

Separate production from staging and archived versions. Development previews, drafts, and comparison pages should not compete with the canonical public route.

  • Verify indexable pages return a successful status and use self-referencing canonicals
  • Keep the sitemap limited to canonical public URLs
  • Confirm redirects, retired routes, drafts, and staging hosts follow the approved policy

Check page-level search signals

Each indexable page needs one clear purpose, a unique title and description, one H1, useful headings, and internal links that match the site architecture.

Structured data should describe visible, supportable content. Do not add reviews, ratings, products, locations, or outcomes that the page does not genuinely present.

  • Compare title, description, canonical, H1, Open Graph, and schema values
  • Use descriptive image alternatives and explicit image dimensions
  • Reject duplicate pages that target the same intent without a real content difference

Test speed, mobile layout, and accessibility

Performance work should begin with measured bottlenecks such as oversized images, blocking assets, unstable layout, or unnecessary scripts. Avoid removing useful content simply to improve a single score.

Test the actual responsive boundaries, keyboard path, focus visibility, form labels, heading order, and contrast. Search visibility is not useful if customers cannot read or complete the page.

  • Serve appropriately sized modern images with stable dimensions
  • Check layout shift, overflow, interaction targets, and browser errors
  • Keep important content and actions available without fragile animation or third-party scripts

Turn findings into a repair sequence

Group issues by impact and dependency. Fix blocked or conflicting canonical pages before polishing low-value metadata, and repair broken conversion paths before producing additional content.

Record the source change, test evidence, deployment, and live verification. A repeatable audit should make it clear what changed and what still needs a business decision.

  • Prioritize index control, broken routes, and conflicting canonical signals
  • Next address content clarity, internal links, mobile experience, and conversion defects
  • Re-crawl and verify live pages after release rather than closing from source changes alone

Keep the next step practical

A useful technical audit reduces uncertainty. Confirm the public page set, repair contradictory signals, test the customer experience, and finish with a prioritized release plan that can be verified on the live site.
